content2.content: When creating custom widgets in Flutter, you'll often choose between Stateless and Stateful widgets. Understanding their differences is crucial for building efficient and responsive apps.

content4.content: In Flutter, everything is a widget – buttons, images, layouts, and even the app itself. You can create your own custom widgets by extending either StatelessWidget or StatefulWidget.

content7.content: A StatelessWidget is a widget that never changes once it is built.

content12.content:
Immutable: The properties (fields marked final) of a StatelessWidget cannot change after the widget is created.
No Internal State: It doesn't have any internal state that can be modified during its lifetime.
build() Method: It has a build() method that is called once when the widget is inserted into the widget tree (or when its parent changes its configuration). This method returns a widget tree that describes this part of the UI
Lightweight: Generally simpler and more performant than StatefulWidgets because they don't need to manage state.

content13.content:
For UI elements that are static and don't need to change dynamically.
Examples: An icon, a label with fixed text, a decorative image, a screen title that doesn't change.
When the widget's appearance only depends on the configuration information passed in by its parent and doesn't change internally.

content16.content: A StatefulWidget, on the other hand, is a widget that describes a part of the user interface that can change dynamically during its lifetime. This change can be triggered by user interactions, receiving new data, or internal logic.

content18.content:
Mutable State: It can maintain state that might change.
Two Classes: A StatefulWidget is actually implemented by two classes:
A subclass of StatefulWidget (which is itself immutable, like a StatelessWidget).
A subclass of State which holds the mutable state and the logic to build the widget.
createState() Method: The StatefulWidget class has a createState() method that returns an instance of its associated State class.
State Object: The State object is where the mutable data lives. It persists across rebuilds of the widget.
setState() Method: To tell Flutter that the internal state of a widget has changed (and thus the UI needs to be rebuilt), you call setState(). This triggers a call to the build() method of the State object.
Lifecycle Methods: State objects have several lifecycle methods (e.g., initState(), didUpdateWidget(), dispose(), build()) that allow you to manage resources, initialize state, and react to changes.

content20.content:
For UI elements that need to change based on user input (e.g., a checkbox, a text field, a slider).
When the widget's appearance needs to update in response to data changes (e.g., a counter, a loading animation, data fetched from an API).Any time a widget needs to remember something that can change.

row4: Rebuilt when parent passes new data

content25.content: Analogy: A Painting vs. A Whiteboard

content24.content:
StatelessWidget (The Painting): Imagine a beautiful painting hanging on a wall. Once the artist finishes it, the painting itself doesn't change. Its appearance is fixed. It might be moved to a different wall (parent changes), but the painting's content remains the same.
StatefulWidget (The Whiteboard): Think of a whiteboard in a classroom. You can write on it, erase parts, and draw new things. Its content (state) changes over time based on interactions (someone writing on it). The whiteboard itself (the StatefulWidget part) is the frame and surface, while what's written on it (the State object) is what changes.
